To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the endogenous uncertainty in the benefits of integration can explain the gradualism of international union formation.
the formation of an international union may be gradual, even when it is efficient, because the union members may be uncertain about the benefits of the grand coalition.

(i) the grand coalition is not necessarily the outcome of the bargaining process; (ii) the grand coalition may be weakly efficient; (iii) the core countries may have an incentive to form a bilateral sub-union first; (iv) the peripheral country may have an incentive, in equilibrium, to wait out the formation of the bilateral union; and (v) the core countries’ incentive to expand their sub-union is a function of their uncertainty about the benefits from integration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of international unions as the result of strategic bargaining among countries.
the strategic considerations of countries when they form international unions and the implications of such considerations for the design of supranational institutions.
the strategic interaction between the core and the periphery countries in the formation and enlargement of international institutions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
uncertainty about the benefits and costs of integration is a key factor in understanding why the European Union was formed gradually, and not all at once.
gradualism is a consequence of the strategic interaction among core countries in a world of uncertainty.
the EU is not an efficient union, but rather a coalition that is the result of an ongoing strategic bargaining process between its members.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

uncertainty about the benefits from integration can generate the gradual formation of the grand union in equilibrium, and that the core countries can have an incentive to delay the accession process in order to signal their high resolve.
gradualism is a rational strategy for countries in the formation of international unions.
uncertainty about the benefits from integration can be a powerful mechanism that can explain the observed gradualist approach to international union formation and enlargement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
uncertainty can be a key determinant of the timing of international union formation.
uncertainty about the benefits from union formation may well be an important determinant of the gradualism of the integration process.
gradualist approaches in union enlargement are not necessarily driven by the need for a ‘learning by doing’ process or the ‘preference for diversity’.
